newsitem.title: france: Corsican separatists claim Juppe town hall bombing.
newsitem.headline: Corsican separatists claim Juppe town hall bombing.

text.p: Corsican separatists claimed responsibility on Monday for a bomb attack on Prime Minister Alain Juppe's mayoral office in Bordeaux, raising the spectre of an offensive in mainland France.

In a brief statement to news organisations in the Corsican capital Ajaccio, the so-called "historic wing" of the Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC) said it carried out the Saturday night attack, causing damage but no casualties.
"Claim responsibility for bomb attack at the Bordeaux city hall," the outlawed group said in a short-hand statement, devoid of the usual rambling ideological justifications.
Juppe held emergency consultations with his interior and justice ministers and ordered security stepped up at public buildings in Paris and provincial cities.
The blast was an escalation of the FLNC's long-running, low-intensity struggle for greater autonomy from Paris.
It was an apparent reaction to a clampdown ordered by Juppe when he visited the Mediterranean island in July, following the breakdown of secret talks with the FLNC earlier this year.

The FLNC, estimated to have a few hundred armed followers, has long been taken less seriously than the Irish Republican Army (IRA) fighting British rule in Northern Ireland or the Basque ETA guerrillas in Spain because it confined its action to Corsica and rarely spilled blood.
It has scant popular support and its action has often seemed more theatrical than lethal, on the borderline between politics and organised crime.

There have been more than 80 bomb attacks on government offices and police stations in Corsica since July, but this was only the second on the mainland, after a small device damaged a courthouse in Aix-en-Provence nine days ago.

Security sources said Juppe had been warned just a week ago by the police intelligence agency of the danger of a bomb attack on his Bordeaux mayoral office or the Marseille city hall, where Regional Development Minister Jean-Claude Gaudin is mayor.
There was no apparent increase in security before the blast.

A nationwide security operation, known as "Vigipirate", has been in force since a wave of bombings blamed on Algerian Moslem fundamentalists last year, but the interior ministry had reduced the level of alert in January.

Juppe's office said he asked Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre and Justice Minister Jacques Toubon to do the utmost to speed up the investigation and bring the culprits to justice. The probe was entrusted to the Paris anti-terrorist prosecutor.

Juppe ordered the crackdown in July after all parties accused Paris of being soft on the separatists' 20-year-old bombing campaign and allowing gunmen to roam the lawless island unchecked and engage in tit-for-tat sectarian killings.
Several suspects have since been detained, angering separatists who accused Juppe of reneging on promises made in the secret "peace process".

As if to reassure citizens that the police were not powerless, the interior ministry announced in a statement that police had seized a weapons cache in southern Corsica on Monday and arrested two suspects.
While condemning the Bordeaux bombing, opposition Socialists said the government had brought the violence upon itself.
"It long conducted secret talks with secret groups and today it seems to be paying a high price since nothing came from the talks," Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande said.
Juppe said in an television interview on Sunday night he would stick to a policy of firmness towards the separatists.
"The state cannot yield and must not be intimidated. We will remain fully determined regarding Corsica," he said.
